title: Jeremiah 22:1–9
context: The LORD tells Jeremiah to go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there. Jeremiah is to call the king, his servants, and the people to execute justice and righteousness, rescue the robbed from the oppressor, and do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow, nor shed innocent blood (compare 7:6). If they obey, kings on David’s throne will continue to enter the palace gates; if not, the LORD swears by himself that the house will become a desolation (compare 17:25). The LORD compares the royal house to Gilead and the summit of Lebanon, yet says he will make it a wilderness and send destroyers to cut down its choice cedars. Passing nations will ask why the LORD has done this, and the answer will be that the people abandoned his covenant and served other gods, an exchange that echoes Deuteronomy 29:24–26 and 1 Kings 9:8–9. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the oracle in its historical frame as a call to royal justice with real consequences, and as shared ground about God’s concern for the vulnerable.

verses.text: The LORD said, “Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak this word there:
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD sending Jeremiah down to the king’s house to speak his word there. The prophet brings God’s message to the center of power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD directing his prophet to the palace. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that kings are answerable to God’s word.

verses.text: ‘Hear the LORD’s word, king of Judah, who sits on David’s throne—you, your servants, and your people who enter in by these gates.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king of Judah, his servants, and the people called to hear the LORD’s word. All share responsibility for justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king addressed as one who sits on David’s throne under God’s covenant. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to the whole royal household.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Execute justice and righteousness, and deliver him who is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor. Do no wrong. Do no violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow. Don’t shed innocent blood in this place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD commanding justice, rescue for the robbed, and protection for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The call is concrete and urgent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s enduring concern for the vulnerable (compare Jeremiah 7:6; James 1:27). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground, kept in its royal setting.

verses.text: For if you do this thing indeed, then kings sitting on David’s throne will enter in by the gates of this house, riding in chariots and on horses—they, their servants, and their people.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the promise that if the king obeys, David’s line will continue to enter the palace gates. Obedience brings real blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conditional promise as part of God’s covenant dealings with David’s house (compare Jeremiah 17:25). Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame.

verses.text: But if you will not hear these words, I swear by myself,” says the LORD, “that this house will become a desolation.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD swearing by himself that the house will become a desolation if they refuse to hear. The warning is serious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s oath underscoring the certainty of judgment on disobedience. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober warning to the royal house.

verses.text: For the LORD says concerning the house of the king of Judah: “You are Gilead to me, the head of Lebanon. Yet surely I will make you a wilderness, cities which are not inhabited.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD comparing the royal house to Gilead and the summit of Lebanon, yet warning it will become a wilderness. Glory does not guarantee safety.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the images of beauty and height reversed in judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against trusting in splendor.

verses.text: I will prepare destroyers against you, everyone with his weapons, and they will cut down your choice cedars, and cast them into the fire.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD preparing destroyers to cut down the choice cedars and cast them into the fire. The palace’s pride will be burned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cedars as a likely image of the royal buildings (compare 1 Kings 7:2). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the oracle’s sober warning.

verses.text: “Many nations will pass by this city, and they will each ask his neighbor, ‘Why has the LORD done this to this great city?’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see many nations passing the ruined city and asking why the LORD has done this. The judgment will be visible to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene echoing Deuteronomy 29:24 and 1 Kings 9:8. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s dealings with his people are a witness to the nations.

verses.text: Then they will answer, ‘Because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD their God, worshiped other gods, and served them.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the answer that the people abandoned the LORD’s covenant and served other gods. The cause of judgment is unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant breaking named as the root of the disaster (compare 1 Kings 9:9). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about the seriousness of idolatry.
